newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai army to press for bigger fund allocation.
newsitem.headline: Thai army to press for bigger fund allocation.

text.p: The influential Thai army will press for sharply higher budget allocations despite new Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh's pledge to slow down defence spending, a senior army source said on Tuesday.

The army would seek an 80-billion-baht ($3.2-billion) budget allocation for fiscal 1997/98 (October-September) despite calls to curb its spending to reduce Thailand's widening current account deficit, he told Reuters.
Propoals for fiscal 1998 funding needs of the army must be presented to the Budget Bureau later this week, said the source, who declined to be identified.
The army received more than 50 billion baht in funding for fiscal 1997.
Authorities expect Thailand's current account deficit, one of the highest in the region, to grow to 8.2 percent of gross domestic product this year compared with 8.1 percent in 1995.
Chavalit, who is also defence minister, has vowed to curb heavy fund outflows from the country to reduce that deficit.

"The 1998 budget requirement will be divided into 65 percent for fixed operating costs and maintenance and 35 percent for developing the strength of the army through purchase of weapons," the army source said.

"The army is well aware of the problem of the trade deficit and current account deficit but we still have to propose our real needs to the government. It is up to the higher authorities to consider them," he added.

The army wants to buy 50,000 rifles to replace the ageing U.S.-made M16As currently in use, and a fleet of tanks to replace the British-made Scorpion light tanks now deployed for more than 20 years, he said.
